classification.difficultyReason: Apply the supplied definition of a polyhedron to distinguish flat polygonal faces from curved surfaces and solids pierced by holes.

questions.mappingNote: Classifying these six solids applies the taught face and hole criteria. compare-prisms-pyramids is the closest supplied catalogue skill for comparing solid properties.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 defines a polyhedron as a solid wholly bounded by flat simple polygonal faces and not pierced by holes. Page 3 contrasts spheres, cylinders and cones with polyhedra.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the supplied definition of a polyhedron to distinguish flat polygonal faces from curved surfaces and solids pierced by holes.

classification.difficultyReason: Count faces, edges and vertices of five supplied solids, including hidden features.

questions.mappingNote: Counting the structural features of supplied prisms and pyramids is the directly assessed component of construct-3d-models; no construction or Euler-formula calculation is requested.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 defines faces, edges and vertices and counts these on a quadrilateral pyramid. Count visible and hidden features systematically, separating base or end features from lateral features.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Count faces, edges and vertices of five supplied solids, including hidden features.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the prism definition to perspective drawings, distinguishing an irregular but uniform prism from a block whose local recess changes its cross-section. This requires checking spatial structure beyond recognising familiar solids.

questions.mappingNote: Each of the seven parts asks for prism recognition. The curved solid, two pyramids and local recess test the defining properties rather than naming bases.
questions.methodNote: Use the definition of a polyhedron and the prism definition: two identical parallel polygonal faces with the remaining faces parallelograms. Compare uniform cross-sections and distinguish pyramids.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise polygonal prisms, distinguishing curved surfaces, pyramids and a locally recessed block.

classification.difficultyReason: Organise prism faces, edges and vertices into ends and connecting features, generalise the counts to expressions in n, then substitute and simplify. The completed numerical cases and explicit intermediate prompts scaffold the generalisation.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed generalisation is Euler's formula, supported by solid counting and algebraic expressions.
questions.methodNote: Count faces, edges and vertices using the definitions and the two identical ends of a prism; form expressions and evaluate V-E+F.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Generalises prism counts algebraically and simplifies Euler's expression.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish base features from those contributed by the apex, express the three counts in terms of n, and simplify V-E+F. The numerical table and separate prompts guide this routine transition from spatial counting to algebra.

questions.mappingNote: Euler's expression is the most advanced assessed skill; naming and skeletal counts support the task.
questions.methodNote: Use the definitions of face, edge and vertex; count the polygonal base and the apex, then generalise and simplify V-E+F.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Counts pyramid features, generalises in n and verifies Euler's expression.

classification.difficultyReason: Count features systematically in the Platonic-solid drawings, accounting for hidden features and avoiding duplicate counts, then substitute into the supplied expression. The more complex solids require spatial organisation, but no generalisation or new relationship is requested.

questions.mappingNote: Euler's formula is the closest catalogue skill for evaluating V − E + F; counting solid features is supporting content.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 names and depicts all five Platonic solids. Page 3 defines faces, edges and vertices. Count these features, including hidden ones, then substitute the counts into V − E + F; page 6 supplies the aggregate result after the question.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Count faces, edges and vertices of five Platonic solids, then evaluate the same expression for each.

classification.difficultyReason: Copy the supplied outlines, recesses and unit divisions onto the three lattice directions, preserving relative lengths. Even the branched solid requires direct reproduction rather than a new viewpoint or hidden-structure inference.

questions.mappingNote: construct-3d-models is the nearest catalogue skill for copying the supplied three-dimensional projection. No hidden cube count, volume or orthographic-view task is assessed.
questions.methodNote: Use the vertical and two sloping directions of an isometric lattice, keeping equal unit steps and copying the visible outline and unit divisions. Source8 supplies the common instruction; source9 continues d–f.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Reproduces each supplied unit-divided solid on an isometric lattice, preserving directions and visible recesses.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate each solid into labelled orthographic views, deciding which heights overlap and which face boundaries remain visible. The stepped and recessed solids require coordinating footprint, height and viewing direction using the taught projection method.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed task is constructing orthographic views of solids, including composite solids.
questions.methodNote: Use the labelled viewing direction for each elevation and look directly down for the plan; Example 1 retains visible face boundaries.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret indicated viewing directions and represent six solids in three orthographic views.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish genuinely different cube arrangements from rotations, then recognise that a three-cube bend in another plane is still an L-shaped prism. The second part requires extending the supplied same-level classification to unrestricted orientations.

questions.mappingNote: Classifying the constructed cube objects by the defining property of a prism is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: A prism has identical parallel end faces and a uniform cross-section. Isometric drawings can represent the same cube object in different orientations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Enumerate connected cube solids, distinguish rotations from different objects, and identify uniform cross-sections.

classification.difficultyReason: Generate the four missing face-connected arrangements while excluding rotations and mirror duplicates, including configurations extending in three dimensions. Then test for uniform cross-section in any orientation to distinguish the two non-prisms.

questions.mappingNote: Classifying the constructed cube objects by the defining property of a prism is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: A prism has identical parallel end faces and a uniform cross-section. Isometric drawings can represent the same cube object in different orientations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Enumerate connected cube solids, distinguish rotations from different objects, and identify uniform cross-sections.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose alternative orientations and redraw each assembly while preserving dimensions and cube connections. The bent base with a tall column requires tracking its right-angle turn through rotation and deciding which edges remain visible.

questions.mappingNote: Students construct alternative spatial views of cube assemblies.
questions.methodNote: Use isometric directions to represent perpendicular cube edges; rotating a solid changes its drawing while preserving its structure.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Rotate each cube assembly mentally and preserve its cube count, connections and dimensions in two new isometric views.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret the hidden edges to identify and name the prism's faces, construct projections from specified directions, and redraw the wedge from another viewpoint. Preserving triangular-end connections and visibility is the hardest demand; Euler verification is direct counting and substitution.

questions.mappingNote: Views of prisms is the main assessed skill because parts c and d require representations from different viewpoints. Identification, face counting and Euler verification are supporting skills.
questions.methodNote: Use the definitions of triangular prisms, faces, edges and vertices; draw orthographic outlines from the specified directions and a different isometric view; count V, E and F and substitute into Euler's formula.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines identification and face naming with orthographic views, an alternative isometric drawing and an Euler check.

classification.difficultyReason: Coordinate the raised rear section and front notch across four projections, distinguishing visible internal edges from features concealed in the back view. Then apply the uniform-cross-section definition to classify the complete solid.

questions.mappingNote: The four requested projections directly assess views-of-prisms; deciding whether the stepped, notched object is a prism additionally uses uniform cross-section.
questions.methodNote: Page 6 defines plan, front, rear and side views as direct observations. Pages 7–8 connect isometric drawings with orthographic views and retain visible internal edges. Page 3 identifies prisms by identical parallel ends and uniform cross-section.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires four orthographic views of a stepped solid with a front notch, followed by recognition that its cross-section is not uniform.

classification.difficultyReason: Select two new viewpoints for each assembly and transfer the L-shaped base and stacked cube consistently to isometric paper. This requires tracking arm lengths, the stack's attachment point and visible subdivisions through routine spatial rotations.

questions.mappingNote: The task asks for alternative isometric representations rather than orthogonal elevations; sketch-3d-views is the closest supplied skill.
questions.methodNote: Pages 7–8 explain isometric drawings using three parallel edge directions, equal unit-cube edges and different orientations of the same solid.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Visualise each cube assembly from two different isometric viewpoints while preserving its connected cubes.

classification.difficultyReason: Use Euler’s formula to infer face counts, then identify solids from their faces, edges and vertices, including a less familiar polyhedron.

questions.mappingNote: Each part substitutes the supplied vertex and edge counts into Euler’s formula, solves for the face count, and identifies a compatible polyhedron. Part c requires a descriptive identification beyond the familiar prism and pyramid examples.
questions.methodNote: Page 6 establishes Euler’s formula by counting faces, edges and vertices. Pages 2–3 define polyhedra and their parts and identify familiar solids. Pages 7–8 concern drawing solids and introduce no alternative calculation method for this question.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use Euler’s formula to infer face counts, then identify solids from their faces, edges and vertices, including a less familiar polyhedron.

classification.difficultyReason: Infer a pyramid's base from matching face and vertex counts, then name the solid.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly assess naming a pyramid from its face and vertex properties. Counting the components independently confirms each name.
questions.methodNote: Identify faces and vertices, count the base vertices and apex, and name a pyramid by its polygonal base. Page 6 states Euler’s formula; pages 7–8 concern drawing views and supply no additional method needed here.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Infer a pyramid's base from matching face and vertex counts, then name the solid.

classification.difficultyReason: Generalise the illustrated joined solid by separating exterior faces, edge groups and vertex groups, then reverse the counts to identify two different polyhedra. The supplied example and Euler check scaffold the reasoning.

questions.mappingNote: Euler’s formula is the shared challenge instruction and checks the generalised counts; constructing and naming prisms and pyramids support the drawing and identification parts.
questions.methodNote: Use the definitions of faces, edges and vertices, count exterior components of joined prisms and pyramids, generalise counts for an n-sided base, and check with Euler’s formula. Drawing evidence uses solid visible edges and dashed concealed edges.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Generalise the face, edge and vertex counts of an extended pyramid and identify different solids with matching counts.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct a prism from specified cross-section properties and visualise assemblies into a hexagonal prism and a honeycomb.

questions.mappingNote: Page 3 directly supplies the prism and uniform-cross-section definitions. Pages 6–8 supply drawing and visualisation context. The assessed progression is identifying an isosceles trapezium cross-section, combining two such prisms and assembling regular hexagonal prisms.
questions.methodNote: Use identical parallel polygonal ends and uniform cross-section to construct prisms. Represent corresponding edges consistently in a three-dimensional sketch, with hidden edges dashed.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a prism from specified cross-section properties and visualise assemblies into a hexagonal prism and a honeycomb.

classification.difficultyReason: The hardest demand is discovering, without a construction hint, that four alternate parallelepiped vertices form a tetrahedron whose edges are face diagonals. The midpoint construction also requires spatial interpretation to recognise the resulting octahedron.

questions.mappingNote: The four related construction tasks principally assess constructing and recognising solids; part a additionally evaluates Euler’s formula.
questions.methodNote: Identify faces, edges and vertices; use Euler’s formula and sketches with dashed hidden edges. Preserve parallel edges when drawing solids.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Visualise joined and inscribed solids, construct their sketches, and count faces, edges and vertices.

classification.difficultyReason: Visualise six congruent square pyramids sharing an interior apex and communicate the decomposition in a drawing.

questions.mappingNote: Constructing and interpreting a decomposition into square pyramids most closely matches construct-3d-models. The isometric drawing guidance supports communicating the construction; Euler calculations are not requested in this item.
questions.methodNote: Use the source’s cube and pyramid representations, recognising square bases and a common apex, and represent the solid with visible and hidden edges.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Visualise six congruent square pyramids sharing an interior apex and communicate the decomposition in a drawing.
